           INTERVENOR LAZY B LAND COMPANY, LLC'S INITIAL BRIEF

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES (ALJ)                                                 AND
COMMISSIONERS OF THE TEXAS PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION:


                                       I. INTRODUCTION

1. COME NOW, Intervenor Lazy B Land Company, LLC, by and through its Managing Member
   Benjamin Tanner (collectively "Lazy B"), and files this Initial Brief after the close of evidence
   at the hearing on the merits in the above-captioned proceeding. Lazy B respectfully requests
   that the Administrative Law Judges (ALJs) and the Public Utility Commission of Texas
   (Commission) deny any route utilizing proposed Link G73, or in the alternative, require
   substantial rerouting and professional cultural-resource review before any ground disturbance
   occurs.

2. Lazy B Land Company, LLC, is the owner of a 613.8-acre ranch in Bell County, Texas,
   identified as Tract 5302 on the project's ArcGIS map. The ranch lies between Texas Highway
   195 and Wolfridge Road (Bell County Tax ID No. 32688; legal description: A1142BC B S
   DECHARD, 4, ACRES 613.778). Intervenor Benjamin Tanner purchased the property through
   Lazy B in 2015 from the Eisenberg family, who had owned it for many decades prior.

3. Proposed Link G73 traverses the property across virtually its entire length, running parallel to
   and within approximately 100 feet of the property's defining natural feature: a spring-fed creek,
   waterfall, and natural limestone sink locally known as the "Indian Bathtub." This feature is the
   heart of the property's primary use. It is a no-cost, full-access nature and agritourism retreat for
   over a dozen veterans and disabled veterans of the United States Armed Forces. It has been
   used in that capacity continuously since 2015, with no profit or salary ever drawn by anyone
   involved.

4. The construction of a 765-kV transmission line along Link G73 would cause severe, likely
   irreversible harm across multiple dimensions: (1) destruction of the property's primary and
   current use; (2) likely desecration of an undisturbed, high-sensitivity archeological area
   containing Archaic Native American cultural materials, including burned-rock midden features
   and projectile points; (3) significant environmental and aesthetic harm to a unique riparian and
   geological landscape; and (4) material diminution of property value.

5. Crucially, these harms were foreseeable and preventable. As detailed below, Applicants
   admitted on the record that Link G73 was a "new link" added to the project after the initial
   public participation meetings, and that G73 landowners within 500 feet of the proposed

                                             Page 2 of 8
    centerline were not mailed notice prior to those meetings as required by 16 Tex. Admin. Code
   § 22.52(a)(4). This failure denied Lazy B and its neighbors their statutory right to early-stage
   participation and cannot be cured retroactively.


      II. PROCEDURAL AND NOTICE VIOLATIONS — LINK G73 WAS ADDED
                      WITHOUT REQUIRED NOTICE

6. Title 16, Texas Administrative Code § 22.52(a)(4) requires that applicants, prior to filing a
   CCN application, hold at least one public meeting and mail first-class notice to the owner of
   land within 500 feet of the proposed route. The rule further provides that "[f]ailure to provide
   notice in accordance with this section will be cause for day-for-day extension of deadlines for
   intervention and for commission action on the application." The language is mandatory and
   self-executing.

7. During cross-examination on June 8, 2026, the first day of the hearing on the merits, Benjamin
   Tanner asked Applicants' representative directly: "A majority of link G-73 Landowners did not
   receive mail notice of the project until late March, 2026, correct?" The representative
   responded: "Yes, since that was an added link, after public participation meetings, that is
   correct." This admission is now part of the evidentiary record and is dispositive on the notice
   question.

8. The three pre-application public participation meetings were held on June 16, 2025 in Salado,
   June 17, 2025 in Lampasas, and June 18, 2025 in Menard. Lazy B and the other G73
   landowners received no mail notice of any of these meetings. Their first direct notification
   came in late March 2026, upon filing of the application, approximately nine months after the
   public meetings had already occurred, by which time the preliminary route selections had
   already been substantially fixed.

9. The harm from this failure is structural. Had Lazy B received timely notice, it would have had
   the opportunity to appear at the June 2025 public meetings, describe the spring-fed creek, the
   off-grid cabin, the veteran retreat use, and the presence of extensive archeological materials,
   and potentially influence the route decision before Link G73 was ever selected. That
   opportunity was permanently foreclosed. The remedy, striking Link G73 from consideration
   or granting day-for-day relief, is mandated by the rule's text and by basic principles of due
   process.

10. Lazy B hereby incorporates and adopts the legal arguments set forth in the G73 Landowners'
    Motion to Strike Link G73 from Consideration, or in the Alternative, for Day-for-Day
    Extension of Deadlines Pursuant to 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 22.52(a)(4), filed June 10, 2026
    (Item No. on file with the Commission), and urges the ALJs to recommend that Link G73 be
    stricken from further consideration in this proceeding.


                                           Page 3 of 8
                 III. PROPERTY DESCRIPTION AND LAND USE IMPACT

11. The Lazy B property is a 613.8-acre ranch situated between Texas Highway 195 and Wolfridge
    Road in Bell County. The property has been held by Lazy B since 2015 and was held by the
    Eisenberg family for many decades before that. It has never been disturbed by industrial or
    commercial development, and no transmission line, pipeline, or major utility corridor has ever
    crossed it.

12. The property's most significant natural feature is a spring-fed stream, waterfall, and deep
    natural limestone sink located at the heart of the ranch. This feature is rare and remarkable —
    a clear-water, self-sustaining riparian and geological system that is unique in the region. Link
    G73 runs parallel to this feature in its entirety, with the proposed right-of-way boundary falling
    approximately 100 feet from the waterfall and creek at its closest point.

13. The property's primary and effectively sole use since purchase has been as a full-access, no-
    cost nature and agritourism retreat for veterans of the United States Armed Forces, many of
    whom are disabled due to military service. Well over twenty veterans have used the property
    in this capacity over the course of more than ten years. Not a single person has ever profited
    from or drawn any salary in connection with this use. This use is not incidental or occasional.
    It is an intentional current purpose for which the property is held and managed.

14. The proposed 765-kV transmission corridor would cause material impairment of this veteran
    retreat use through multiple mechanisms. The visual impacts of a large-scale transmission
    structure adjacent to the creek, waterfall, and limestone sink — the only areas where veterans
    gather and recreate — would fundamentally alter and effectively destroy the secluded, natural
    character that makes the property suitable for this purpose. The cleared right-of-way,
    maintenance access requirements, noise during construction and operation, and permanent
    presence of transmission infrastructure would render the property unsuitable for the quiet,
    nature-based therapeutic retreat it currently provides.

15. In addition to the veteran retreat use, the property contains an off-grid cabin that Intervenor
    Benjamin Tanner constructed by hand between 2019 and 2024. This structure is located
    approximately 100 feet from the proposed G73 link. The proposed right-of-way also runs
    virtually over the top of a neighboring landowner's newly constructed residence at the north
    boundary of the property — a structure that did not appear on the ArcGIS map published by
    Applicants, suggesting that it was not reflected in the project's habitation mapping and was not
    accounted for in Applicants' review.

16. The land is currently under active wildlife management and is maintained in a natural state
    without livestock. The right-of-way clearing required by a 765-kV corridor would remove

                                             Page 4 of 8
    native habitat, including the riparian corridor associated with the spring-fed creek. Native
   Texas species including white-tailed deer, wild turkey, and riparian wildlife that depend on
   this habitat corridor would be materially harmed. The wildlife management program that
   characterizes the property's current use would no longer be viable in its present form.

17. In the opinion of Intervenor Benjamin Tanner, Link G73 will materially reduce the value of
    the 613-acre property by bisecting it, placing a major transmission corridor adjacent to its most
    valuable natural feature, reducing development flexibility, and permanently impairing the
    recreational, therapeutic, and retreat use that defines the property's purpose. These losses are
    not compensable through an easement payment; the veteran retreat that the property hosts
    cannot simply be relocated.


 IV. CULTURAL, HISTORICAL, AND ARCHAEOLOGICAL RESOURCE IMPACTS

18. The Lazy B property contains extensive evidence of prehistoric Native American occupation.
    The cultural materials observed on the property include burned-rock midden features, chert
    debitage, projectile points, inscribed rocks, and other cultural materials concentrated along and
    adjacent to the spring-fed creek, waterfall, and limestone feature. These materials are
    consistent with intensive Archaic-period occupation of a permanent water source in Central
    Texas.

19. The significance of this potential archeological resource is underscored by the property's
    proximity to the Gault Archaeological Site, one of the most significant and extensively studied
    prehistoric sites in North American archaeology, located approximately six miles away near
    Florence, Texas. The property's geological setting, a spring-fed creek in a limestone karst
    environment, is precisely the type of setting associated with high-density Archaic occupations
    throughout the Central Texas region. The density of surface cultural materials observed on the
    Lazy B property suggests the potential for deep, intact subsurface archaeological deposits.

20. Intervenor Benjamin Tanner was also informed by a longtime user of the property with ties to
    the former owner that approximately fifteen years ago, a Texas State University archaeologist
    visited the property and commented that it appeared to contain an unusually large number of
    artifacts. While this is not a formal survey finding, it is consistent with Lazy B's own
    observations and further supports the characterization of the property as a high-sensitivity
    archaeological area.

21. The property has intentionally not been extensively disturbed, excavated, or explored by Lazy
    B or, to the best of Lazy B's knowledge, by any prior owner. The cultural materials observed
    on the surface are therefore likely the visible portion of a much larger undisturbed subsurface
    assemblage. Construction of a 765-kV transmission corridor through this area — involving
    heavy equipment, deep anchor installations, and extensive ground disturbance — would


                                            Page 5 of 8
    present an acute and likely irreversible risk to the integrity of these deposits, and potentially to
   intact human burials associated with Archaic occupations of this type.

22. Lazy B does not ask the Commission to make a formal archeological determination based
    solely on lay testimony. Rather, Lazy B asks the Commission to apply the principle of
    avoidance — a standard principle in cultural resource management — and decline to route a
    765-kV transmission line through an area with obvious and documented cultural-resource
    sensitivity, without first requiring a professional cultural resources survey and consultation
    with the Texas Historical Commission (THC) as contemplated by the Texas Antiquities Code,
    Tex. Nat. Res. Code ch. 191, and applicable agency rules at 13 Tex. Admin. Code § 26.2.

23. Applicants' cultural resources review of the Link G73 corridor was inadequate. Applicants'
    witnesses admitted that their review of route links was conducted primarily through desktop
    analysis of aerial and geophysical maps, or from observations made along main highways. The
    G73 corridor runs far from any public road, through undisturbed land with dense surface
    cultural materials concentrated around a spring-fed water source. No such desktop review
    could be adequate to evaluate the archaeological sensitivity of this specific corridor. A site visit
    by a qualified professional would have revealed the significance of this area before the link
    was included in any preferred routing.

24. Applicants received no notice that G73 landowners existed or had concerns until late March
    2026. This means that Applicants never had the opportunity, even had they been inclined, to
    conduct pre-application consultation with affected landowners about cultural resources prior
    to fixing Link G73 as part of their preferred routing. This is a direct consequence of the
    unlawful notice failure described in Section II above, and further supports the conclusion that
    Link G73 should be stricken from consideration.


                    V. ENVIRONMENTAL AND AESTHETIC IMPACTS

25. Link G73 runs parallel to and within approximately 110 feet of the spring-fed creek and
    waterfall that constitutes the Lazy B property's defining natural feature. The construction and
    operation of a 765-kV transmission corridor adjacent to this riparian feature would require
    permanent clearing of native vegetation, long-term maintenance of a power line corridor,
    periodic vegetation management, and ongoing access road maintenance — all of which would
    fragment the native habitat associated with the creek corridor and degrade the ecological
    integrity of the spring-fed stream system.

26. The visual impact of a 765-kV transmission structure in this location would be especially
    severe because the creek, waterfall, and limestone sink are the central areas where people
    gather and experience the property. The property's exceptional value and its suitability as a
    therapeutic environment for disabled veterans derives entirely from its secluded, undisturbed,


                                             Page 6 of 8
    natural character. The permanent installation of a large-scale transmission corridor adjacent to
   this feature would eliminate that character irreversibly.

27. Applicants' own witnesses acknowledged that their environmental assessments were
    conducted primarily by desktop review and highway-observable observations. No field visit to
    the Lazy B property was conducted that would have revealed the spring-fed creek, the
    waterfall, the limestone sink, the dense cultural materials, or the off-grid cabin. This level of
    review is facially insufficient for a property whose most significant features are located far
    from any public road and are not visible from the highway.


                                     VI. NEEDS AND COST

28. Lazy B incorporates and adopts the arguments regarding the needs for this project set forth in
    the testimony and briefs of other intervenors in this proceeding, and urges the Commission to
    independently evaluate whether the need for the proposed 765-kV transmission facilities across
    the Hill Country of Texas has been adequately demonstrated before approving any route.

29. With respect to local need and cost: the proposed transmission line will provide no direct
    benefit to the residents of Bell County or the other counties through which Link G73 passes.
    The project does not increase local generation capacity, does not reduce the cost of electricity
    for local ratepayers, and does not improve local reliability. Its sole function is to transport
    energy from one part of the ERCOT system to another, with the costs of construction ultimately
    passed through to Texas ratepayers for decades.

30. The selection of Link G73 as a preferred routing segment represents a choice to impose severe,
    likely permanent harm on Lazy B Land Company, its veteran users, and a potentially
    irreplaceable archaeological resource, in order to route a transmission line across a corridor
    that Applicants never properly evaluated and for which they never provided legally required
    pre-application notice to affected landowners. This tradeoff, which was never subjected to
    public input from the affected G73 landowners, cannot be justified under PURA's routing
    criteria.


                      VII. CONCLUSION AND PRAYER FOR RELIEF

WHEREFORE, PREMISES CONSIDERED, Intervenor Lazy B Land Company, LLC (Benjamin
Tanner) respectfully requests that the ALJs and the Commission:

   1. STRIKE Link G73 from further consideration as a route or route segment in this
      proceeding, on the basis that Applicants failed to provide mandatory pre-meeting mail


                                            Page 7 of 8
         notice to G73 Landowners in violation of 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 22.52(a)(4), and that
        Applicants' cultural resource review of the Link G73 corridor was inadequate;

    2. In the alternative, DENY any route incorporating Link G73 on the merits, based on the
       severe land use, cultural resource, archaeological, environmental, and aesthetic impacts
       documented in evidence;

    3. In the alternative, require that any route involving Link G73 be modified to avoid the
       spring-fed creek corridor, burned-rock midden areas, artifact-bearing areas, the off-grid
       cabin, and nearby residences, and that no route be approved across this property without a
       professional cultural resources survey and consultation with the Texas Historical
       Commission;

    4. Grant a day-for-day extension of all relevant deadlines pursuant to 16 Tex. Admin. Code
       § 22.52(a)(4), running from June 16, 2025 through the date of effective actual notice to
       G73 Landowners (late March 2026), totaling not less than 283 days; and

    5. Grant Lazy B Land Company, LLC all other relief to which it may be entitled under PURA,
       applicable Commission rules, and applicable law.



                                                                              Respectfully submitted,

                                                                      Lazy B Land Company, LLC
                                                               Benjamin Tanner, Managing Member

   Lazy B property suggests the potential for deep, intact subsurface archaeological deposits.


20. Intervenor Benjamin Tanner was also informed by a longtime user of the property with ties to
    the former owner that approximately fifteen years ago, a Texas State University archaeologist
   visited the property and commented that it appeared to contain an unusually large number of
   artifacts. While this is not a formal survey finding, it is consistent with Lazy B's own
   observations and further supports the characterization of the property as a high-sensitivity
   archaeological area.


21. The property has intentionally not been extensively disturbed, excavated, or explored by Lazy
    B or, to the best of Lazy B's knowledge, by any prior owner. The cultural materials observed
   on the surface are therefore likely the visible portion of a much larger undisturbed subsurface
   assemblage. Construction of a 765-kV transmission corridor through this area - involving
   heavy equipment, deep anchor installations, and extensive ground disturbance - would

    present an acute and likely irreversible risk to the integrity of these deposits, and potentially to
   intact human burials associated with Archaic occupations of this type.


22. Lazy B does not ask the Commission to make a formal archeological determination based
    solely on lay testimony. Rather, Lazy B asks the Commission to apply the principle of
    avoidance - a standard principle in cultural resource management - and decline to route a
   765-kV transmission line through an area with obvious and documented cultural-resource
   sensitivity, without first requiring a professional cultural resources survey and consultation
   with the Texas Historical Commission (THC) as contemplated by the Texas Antiquities Code,

23. Applicants' cultural resources review of the Link G73 corridor was inadequate. Applicants'

                    V. ENVIRONMENTAL AND AESTHETIC IMPACTS


25. Link G73 runs parallel to and within approximately 110 feet of the spring-fed creek and
    waterfall that constitutes the Lazy B property's defining natural feature. The construction and
    operation of a 765-kV transmission corridor adj acent to this riparian feature would require
    permanent clearing of native vegetation, long-term maintenance of a power line corridor,
   periodic vegetation management, and ongoing access road maintenance - all of which would
   fragment the native habitat associated with the creek corridor and degrade the ecological
   integrity of the spring-fed stream system.


26. The visual impact of a 765-kV transmission structure in this location would be especially
    severe because the creek, waterfall, and limestone sink are the central areas where people
   gather and experience the property. The property's exceptional value and its suitability as a
   therapeutic environment for disabled veterans derives entirely from its secluded, undisturbed,

27. Applicants' own witnesses acknowledged that their environmental assessments were

    the Lazy B property was conducted that would have revealed the spring-fed creek, the
    waterfall, the limestone sink, the dense cultural materials, or the off-grid cabin. This level of
    review is facially insufficient for a property whose most significant features are located far

    energy from one part ofthe ERCOT system to another, with the costs of construction ultimately
